name: Hopewell culture
title: The story of the Hopewell culture

text: More than 2,000 years ago, many Native American peoples lived along the rivers of the woodlands of North America.
They lived in small settlements, where they hunted, gathered wild food and grew plants in gardens.
src: a network of Native American peoples who lived along the rivers of the north-eastern and midwestern Eastern Woodlands from about 100 BCE to 500 CE
Many Hopewell communities were small, temporary settlements of one to three households near rivers. They lived by a mixture of hunting, gathering and horticulture

text: They were not one people, but they were linked by trade from Lake Ontario to Florida.
They carried copper, shells and a stone called obsidian from far away, some from as far as Yellowstone.
src: Hopewell was not one people but a widespread set of Native American communities, from Lake Ontario to Florida, linked by trade and shared ceremony
they exchanged copper, mica, shell and obsidian across much of North America / Obsidian at Mound City has been traced to Yellowstone

text: Their craftworkers shaped copper, pearls, shells and sharks' teeth into ornaments.
One mound held more than 200 stone pipes carved in the shapes of animals and birds.
src: They worked grizzly bear teeth, freshwater pearls, sea shells, sharks’ teeth, copper and small amounts of silver into ornaments
The Mound of Pipes at Mound City held more than 200 stone smoking pipes in the form of animals and birds, carved in three dimensions

text: They built huge earthworks, walls of earth in circles, squares and octagons, and buried important people in mounds.
Many of these earthworks survive today, and some in Ohio are a World Heritage Site.
src: geometric enclosures of circles, squares and octagons / burial in a mound was kept for the most important people
Many survive today / the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks are a UNESCO World Heritage Site preserving Ohio Hopewell sites

text: About 1,500 years ago the trade ended, and they stopped building mounds.
But the peoples lived on, and some were ancestors of the Mississippian peoples, who built Cahokia.
src: Around 500 CE the Hopewell exchange ceased, mound building stopped and the characteristic art forms were no longer made
Hopewell peoples did not vanish. The Havana Hopewell are considered ancestral to the groups who formed the Mississippian culture that built Cahokia
